deed: ג'וליוס רוזנוולד ובוקר ט' וושינגטון בונים כ-5,000 בתי ספר לילדים שחורים
title: Julius Rosenwald and Booker T. Washington built thousands of schools for Black children in the southern United States

trailer.text: Julius Rosenwald was a Jewish American who became president of Sears, Roebuck and Company, and the son of Jewish immigrants who fled Germany.
Booker T. Washington was born into slavery in Virginia.
In 1912, Rosenwald gave the Tuskegee Institute a small grant to build six schools for Black students.
According to Britannica, he supported the construction on the condition that each community raise matching funds, and the local communities were the primary drivers of the construction.
In this way, thousands of schools for Black students were built in 15 states, and according to the National Park Service, more than 600,000 students attended them.

glance.label: Founders
glance.value: Julius Rosenwald and Booker T. Washington

glance.label: Where
glance.value: 15 states in the southern United States

glance.label: Alumni
glance.value: Maya Angelou, Medgar Evers, John Lewis

paragraphs.text: According to the National Park Service, before emancipation it was forbidden for most enslaved people in large parts of the United States to learn to read or to go to school.
Many Black students studied in churches, private homes and fields, because they were excluded from the public schools.
In 1909, in Lowndes County, Alabama, white schools received $20 per student.
Black schools there received only $0.67 per student.
In Macon County, where the Tuskegee Institute is located, $14 was spent on each white child and only 20 cents on each Black child.
According to Britannica, in 1900–01 Alabama schools spent an average of only $3.10 per child.
In 1912, Washington wrote to Rosenwald that many of the places of learning in the South were as bad as stables.
He wrote that a teacher cannot work efficiently in them.
Julius Rosenwald was born in Springfield, Illinois, on August 12, 1862, when Lincoln was president of the United States.
The National Park Service describes him as a Jewish American who grew up in Lincoln's shadow and became president of Sears, Roebuck and Company.
According to Britannica, he lived in Chicago.
According to Andrew Feiler in The Forward, he turned Sears into America's largest retailer.
According to the National Archives, as the son of Jewish immigrant parents, Rosenwald had himself experienced prejudice and discrimination.
According to NPR, the 1908 race riot in Springfield, his hometown, made him rethink the treatment of African Americans.
According to Feiler, when asked why he supported African Americans so much, he said that he was interested in America and did not see how it could go ahead if part of its people were left behind.
Booker T. Washington was born into slavery around 1856 in Virginia.
The two met in Chicago at a fundraiser.
According to Google Arts & Culture, they created one of the early collaborations between Jews and African Americans.
According to Encyclopedia.com, Rosenwald ended his term as president of Sears in 1924 and became chairman of the board of directors, a position he held until his death.

stations.title: The first grant and the fund

paragraphs.text: On July 15, 1912, Rosenwald asked Washington in a letter how to divide $25,000 among institutions similar to Tuskegee.
According to Britannica, in 1912 he gave Washington $25,000 to aid Black colleges and preparatory institutions.
According to the New Georgia Encyclopedia, Washington persuaded him to allocate about $2,000 of the sum to an experiment: building elementary schools in rural communities.
In 1912, Rosenwald gave the Tuskegee Institute a small grant to build six schools for Black students.
According to Google Arts & Culture, the first school to open was the Loachapoka School in Lee County, Alabama.
In 1914, Rosenwald donated $30,000 for one hundred schools in Alabama.
In 1917, Rosenwald established the Rosenwald Fund to manage the growing building program.

stations.title: Every community puts money on the table

paragraphs.text: According to Britannica, Rosenwald agreed to support the construction on the condition that each community raise matching funds.
According to Humanities magazine, each school received only seed money, about one third of the construction cost.
Another condition was that the county school board take ownership of the building and maintain it as part of public education.
At the Madison Park school, the cost was $950.
$500 was raised in the Black community, $200 came from white officials and $250 from Rosenwald.
Mt. Zion School in Mars Bluff, South Carolina, cost $3,850.
Black communities held fish fries, bake sales and other events to raise money.
According to Britannica, Black residents came to school-board meetings, demanded meetings with superintendents and worked political connections.
According to the New Georgia Encyclopedia, they were forced to use their limited resources, because public money was diverted to white schools.
According to Britannica, the local communities were the primary drivers of the construction, and the fund came to assist them.
According to Britannica, most of the buildings had two to four classrooms.
They were designed to use natural light, because most of them had no electricity.
According to The 74, the windows and desks were placed so that light would fall over the students' left shoulders, and the writing hand would not cast a shadow.
When the fund moved to Nashville, it hired the white architect Fletcher Dresslar to design new building plans.
The fund also built 217 teachers' homes across the South.
It provided a grant for teachers' pay, so that they would keep working longer.
According to the National Park Service, by 1929 the fund also offered buses for transportation.

According to Britannica, when the program ended in 1932, one out of every five schools in the South was a Rosenwald school, and Britannica does not specify exactly which schools the comparison covered.
According to the National Park Service, more than 600,000 students studied at these schools from the '10s of the 20th century until the '60s.
Federal Reserve researchers estimated that exposure to the schools raised the relative wages of Black people who remained in the South by about 35 percent.
According to the researchers, Black people aged 12 to 16 in 1935 who were exposed to the schools were about 65 percent more likely to migrate to the North by 1940.
According to Feiler, Federal Reserve economists determined that the schools were the most significant factor in narrowing the South's racial education gap between the two World Wars.
According to Tracy Hayes of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the program was the greatest contributor to the education of African Americans in the South in the early 20th century.

stations.title: The alumni, and the buildings that remain

paragraphs.text: Among the schools' alumni are Maya Angelou, Medgar Evers and John Lewis.
According to Feiler, thousands of other alumni became teachers, preachers, farmers, tradespeople and businesspeople.
According to Google Arts & Culture, Webster Wheeler returned from Detroit when he heard that his hometown had received a grant, and built the new school.
Vernon Dahmer attended the Bay Springs school and became head of the NAACP in Forrest County.
After the school closed, he turned it into a center for civil-rights activism, and he was later murdered by the Ku Klux Klan.
Rosenwald made a practice of keeping his name off the projects he funded, and this is one of the reasons he is hardly known today.
He died in 1932, and as he had wished, the Rosenwald Fund was the first foundation to deliberately spend all of its endowment.
According to the National Park Service, many schools closed when states desegregated in the 1950s and 1960s.
In 2022, the United States passed a law directing the National Park Service to study the establishment of a national historical park that would present the schools.
According to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, in 2002 the Rosenwald schools were included in the list of America's 11 Most Endangered Historic Places.

stations.title: What the schools did not change

paragraphs.text: According to Britannica, the schools did not challenge racial segregation, and schooling in them generally ended after eighth grade.
Historian Thomas Hanchett said that the schools educated students to be good farmers, and did not give them the capability to leave rural life.
According to The 74, vocational training at the high schools was deliberately chosen so as not to threaten white domination of the economy.
According to The 74, as many Black people migrated north, local whites often hoped to keep Black labor in the community.
According to Feiler, the modest design was meant partly to save costs and partly to avoid a backlash from local whites, especially arson.
According to The 74, Rosenwald was concerned from the start that the donations would become a way for white officials to divert resources from Black schools.
According to Wikipedia, in the mid-1930s the per-student budget of white schools in the South was still more than five times that of Black schools.

disagreements.question: How many schools had been funded by the time of Washington's death?

versions.says: According to Britannica: when Washington died in 1915, Rosenwald had given matching grants to about 80 schools in three states
According to the New Georgia Encyclopedia: within four years Rosenwald funded the construction of more than 300 rural schools

disagreements.question: How much did the Black communities contribute?

versions.says: According to Britannica: $4.7 million, more than the fund's $4.3 million
According to Wikipedia: $4.8 million for the building of 5,338 schools

disagreements.question: How many shop buildings were built?

versions.says: According to the National Archives: 16 vocational shop buildings, along with 217 teachers' homes
According to the Library of Congress: 163 shop buildings, along with 217 teachers' homes

disagreements.question: How many schools were built in total?

versions.says: According to Britannica: 4,977 schools in 15 states, by 1932
According to the National Archives: more than 5,300 schools, by the end of the program in 1932
According to Feiler: 4,978 schools in 15 Southern and border states
According to The 74: 5,357 schools and associated buildings in 883 counties
According to Wikipedia: 5,388 schools in 883 counties in 15 states, with more than $4 million from the fund

disagreements.question: What share of Black children attended the schools?

versions.says: According to The 74: 663,615 students, more than a fourth of Black children in the South
According to the National Archives: one third of Black children in America, by the end of the program
According to Humanities magazine: one third of rural Black children in 15 Southern states, by 1928

disagreements.question: How many schools have survived to this day?

versions.says: According to Humanities magazine, based on surveys: about eight hundred
According to Google Arts & Culture: about 500 out of 4,978

claims.text: לפי פיילר, כלכלני הפדרל ריזרב קבעו שבתי הספר היו הגורם המשמעותי ביותר בצמצום פער ההשכלה הגזעי בדרום בין שתי מלחמות העולם.
claims.quote: Economists at the Federal Reserve said the Rosenwald Schools were the most significant factor in the narrowing of the South’s racial education gap between World War I and II.

claims.text: לפי טרייסי הייז מהנאמנות הלאומית לשימור היסטורי, תוכנית בתי הספר הייתה התורם הגדול ביותר לחינוך האפרו-אמריקאים בדרום בתחילת המאה ה-20.
claims.quote: The Rosenwald School building program was the single greatest contributor to education of African Americans across the South in the early twentieth century

claims.text: לפי פיילר, אלפי בוגרים נוספים הפכו למורים, לכמרים, לחקלאים, לבעלי מקצוע ולאנשי עסקים.
claims.quote: Thousands of others became teachers, preachers, farmers, tradespeople, and businesspeople

claims.text: לפי גוגל ארטס, ובסטר ווילר חזר מדטרויט לאחר ששמע שעיר הולדתו קיבלה מענק של רוזנוולד ובנה את בית הספר החדש.
claims.quote: Upon hearing that his hometown had been awarded a Rosenwald grant, he returned and built the new school.

claims.text: וורנון דהמר למד בבית הספר ביי ספרינגס, נעשה ראש ה-NAACP במחוז פורסט, ולאחר סגירת בית הספר הפך אותו למרכז פעילות זכויות אזרח; בהמשך נרצח בידי הקו קלוקס קלאן.
claims.quote: He became the head of the NAACP in Forrest County, and when the school closed, Dahmer turned the building into a center for civil-rights activism.

claims.text: רוזנוולד נהג שלא לציין את שמו על הפרויקטים שמימן, וזה תרם לכך שהוא כמעט לא מוכר כיום.
claims.quote: His practice of keeping his name off the projects he funded

claims.text: בהתאם לרצונו של רוזנוולד, שמת ב-1932, קרן רוזנוולד הייתה הקרן הראשונה שהוציאה במכוון את כל ההון שלה.
claims.quote: the Julius Rosenwald Fund became the first foundation to deliberately spend all of its endowment

claims.text: לפי שירות הפארקים הלאומיים, בתי ספר רבים של רוזנוולד נסגרו כשמדינות ביטלו את ההפרדה בשנות ה-50 וה-60.
claims.quote: Many Rosenwald schools closed when the states desegregated public schools in the 1950s and 1960s.

claims.text: ב-2022 העבירה ארצות הברית חוק המורה לשירות הפארקים הלאומיים לבחון הקמת פארק היסטורי לאומי שיציג את בתי הספר.
claims.quote: In 2022 Congress passed a bill directing the National Park Service to study feasilibility of a national historical park preserving and explaining Rosenwald Schools.

claims.text: לפי בריטניקה, בתי הספר לא אתגרו את ההפרדה הגזעית ובדרך כלל הפסיקו ללמד אחרי כיתה ח'.
claims.quote: The schools did not challenge segregation, and they generally stopped educating students after eighth grade.

claims.text: ההיסטוריון תומס הנצ'ט אמר שבתי הספר חינכו את התלמידים להיות חקלאים טובים ולא העניקו להם יכולת לעזוב את החיים הכפריים.
claims.quote: Rosenwald schools educated students to be good farmers, instead of giving them the capability to leave rural life.

claims.text: לפי The 74, ההכשרה המקצועית בבתי הספר התיכוניים נבחרה במכוון כך שלא תאיים על שליטת הלבנים בהיררכיה הכלכלית.
claims.quote: Job training at the new high schools included farming, home economics and shop skills — trades deliberately chosen to not threaten white domination of the economic hierarchy.

claims.text: לפי The 74, עם הגירת שחורים רבים צפונה, לבנים מקומיים קיוו לעיתים לשמור על כוח עבודה שחור בקהילה.
claims.quote: With many blacks joining the Great Migration, local whites often hoped to keep black labor in the community.

claims.text: לפי פיילר, העיצוב הצנוע נועד בחלקו לשלוט בעלויות ובחלקו להימנע מתגובת נגד, ובעיקר הצתות, מצד הלבנים המקומיים.
claims.quote: Such humility was in part to control costs and in part to avoid provoking a backlash, specifically arson, from the local white citizenry.

claims.text: לפי The 74, רוזנוולד חשש מההתחלה שהפילנתרופיה תהפוך למנגנון שבו פקידים לבנים מסיטים משאבים מבתי ספר שחורים.
claims.quote: From the start, Rosenwald was concerned that philanthropy not become a mechanism for white officials to divert resources from black schools.

claims.text: לפי ויקיפדיה, בשנות ה-30 המאוחרות תקציב לתלמיד בבתי ספר לבנים בדרום היה גבוה פי יותר מחמישה מזה של בתי ספר שחורים.
claims.quote: Despite this program, by the mid-1930s white schools in the South had a budget per student more than five times that of black schools

claims.text: לפי שירות הפארקים הלאומיים, האנציקלופדיה של בריטניקה: כשוושינגטון מת ב-1915 העניק רוזנוולד מענקים תואמים לכ-80 בתי ספר שחורים בשלוש מדינות.
claims.quote: By the time of Washington’s death, in 1915, Rosenwald had given matching grants for some 80 Black schools in three states.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה של ג'ורג'יה, במהלך ארבע שנים רוזנוולד מימן בנייה של יותר מ-300 בתי ספר כפריים.
claims.quote: over the next four years Rosenwald contributed private funds for the construction of more than 300 rural school buildings in southern states

claims.text: לפי ויקיפדיה, קהילות אפרו-אמריקאיות תרמו 4.8 מיליון דולר לבניית 5,338 בתי ספר.
claims.quote: African American communities contributed $4.8 million to the building of 5,338 schools throughout the South.

claims.text: לפי הארכיון הלאומי, מענקי רוזנוולד שימשו לבניית 217 בתי מורים ו-16 מבני סדנה מקצועיים.
claims.quote: Grants from Rosenwald were also used to build 217 houses for teachers, 16 vocational shop buildings, and several libraries

claims.text: לפי ספריית הקונגרס, בסיום התוכנית ב-1932 נבנו 4,977 בתי ספר, 217 בתי מורים ו-163 מבני סדנה.
claims.quote: it had produced 4,977 new schools, 217 teachers’ homes, and 163 shop buildings.

claims.text: לפי בריטניקה, עד 1932 הוביל המפעל לבניית 4,977 בתי ספר ב-15 מדינות.
claims.quote: By 1932, when the building program ended, it had been responsible for the construction of 4,977 schools spanning 15 states.

claims.text: לפי הארכיון הלאומי, עד סיום התוכנית ב-1932 נבנו בדרום האמריקאי למעלה מ-5,300 בתי ספר.
claims.quote: By the time the program ended in 1932, over 5,300 schools had been constructed across the American south.

claims.text: לפי The 74, המפעל סייע ליצור 5,357 בתי ספר ומבנים נלווים ב-883 מחוזות.
claims.quote: it had helped to create 5,357 schools and associated buildings in 883 counties that educated 663,615 students

claims.text: לפי ויקיפדיה, הקרן הוציאה יותר מ-4 מיליון דולר לבניית 5,388 בתי ספר, 217 בתי מורים ו-163 מבני סדנה ב-883 מחוזות ב-15 מדינות.
claims.quote: the fund spent more than $4 million to build 5,388 schools, 217 teacher homes, and 163 shop buildings in 883 counties in 15 states, from Maryland to Texas.

claims.text: לפי The 74, בתי הספר חינכו 663,615 תלמידים, יותר מרבע מהילדים השחורים בדרום.
claims.quote: more than a fourth of black children in the South

claims.text: לפי הארכיון הלאומי, עד סיום התוכנית חונך שליש מהילדים השחורים באמריקה בבית ספר של רוזנוולד.
claims.quote: one-third of black children in America overall were educated within a Rosenwald School

claims.text: לפי מגזין Humanities, עד 1928 למד שליש מכלל הילדים השחורים הכפריים בחמש עשרה מדינות דרומיות בבתי ספר של רוזנוולד.
claims.quote: By 1928, one-third of all rural black children in fifteen Southern states attended Rosenwald schools.

claims.text: לפי מגזין Humanities, לפי סקרים כשמונה מאות בתי ספר עדיין עומדים.
claims.quote: Survey data estimates that about eight hundred are still standing.

claims.text: לפי גוגל ארטס, מתוך 4,978 בתי הספר המקוריים כ-500 שרדו.
claims.quote: Of the original 4,978 Rosenwald Schools, about 500 survive.

claims.text: לפי גוגל ארטס, כשהמימון הסופי לבית ספר במחוז מריוות'ר חסר 1,000 דולר, רוזוולט כתב צ'ק אישי לסגירת הפער.
claims.quote: When the final funding came up $1,000 short, Roosevelt wrote a personal check to close the gap.

claims.text: לפי Encyclopedia.com, רוזנוולד סיים את כהונתו כנשיא סירס ב-1924 והיה ליו"ר הדירקטוריון, תפקיד שמילא עד מותו.
claims.quote: He ended his term as president in 1924 and became chairman of the board of directors, a position he held until he died.

claims.text: לפי הקרן הלאומית לשימור היסטורי (National Trust for Historic Preservation), ב-2002 נכללו בתי הספר של רוזנוולד ברשימת 11 האתרים ההיסטוריים בסכנה הגדולה ביותר באמריקה.
claims.quote: In 2002, the National Trust named Rosenwald Schools to its list of America’s 11 Most Endangered Historic Places.
